name: Jesus
bio:
Jesus Christ, descended from Abraham and David through Joseph's line, was conceived by the Holy Spirit and born to Mary while she was engaged to Joseph. An angel instructed Joseph to name him Jesus, "for he will save his people from their sins," fulfilling the ancient prophecy of a virgin-born son called Immanuel, "God with us" (Matthew 1:1-25). His birth, ministry, death, and resurrection are told in full across the four Gospels. Herod the Great, troubled by reports of a newborn King of the Jews, ordered the massacre of young boys in Bethlehem after wise men following a star came seeking him; Joseph, warned by an angel, had already fled with Mary and the infant Jesus to Egypt, returning to settle in Nazareth only after Herod's death (Matthew 2:1-23). As an adult, Jesus came from Galilee to be baptized by John the Baptist in the Jordan; when John objected that he was unworthy to baptize him, Jesus insisted it was necessary to fulfill all righteousness. As he came up from the water, the Spirit descended on him like a dove and a voice from heaven declared him God's beloved Son (Matthew 3:13-17).

 After fasting forty days in the wilderness, Jesus was tempted three times by the devil — to turn stones to bread, to test God by jumping from the temple, and to worship the devil for worldly power — and refuted each temptation with Scripture, after which angels ministered to him. When he heard John the Baptist had been imprisoned, Jesus moved to Capernaum in Galilee, began preaching repentance, and called Simon Peter, Andrew, James, and John away from their fishing nets to follow him, going on to teach, preach, and heal throughout Galilee to large crowds (Matthew 4:1-25).

## 📖 Core Story: The Sermon on the Mount

Jesus delivered an extended teaching to his disciples and the crowds, opening with the Beatitudes' blessings on the humble, grieving, and persecuted. He taught that he came to fulfill rather than abolish the Law, intensifying its demands by locating sin in the heart (anger as a seed of murder, lust as a seed of adultery) and calling his followers to radical love, including love for enemies, rather than mere retaliation or legalism. He warned against showing off religious devotion for others' approval, taught the Lord's Prayer, and urged trust in God's provision over anxiety about material needs, noting that not even Solomon in all his splendor was dressed as beautifully as a wildflower God clothes. He closed by warning against false prophets and hollow profession, and with the parable of building on rock versus sand, leaving the crowds astonished at his authority, unlike that of their own scribes (Matthew 5:1-7:29).

## 📖 Core Story: Early Miracles

Coming down from the mountain, Jesus healed a leper with a touch, then healed a Roman centurion's servant from a distance after the centurion expressed remarkable faith that Jesus needed only to speak the word; Jesus marveled at this gentile's faith exceeding any he had found in Israel. He healed Peter's mother-in-law of a fever in Peter's own house, and cast out many demons and healed the sick that evening, fulfilling Isaiah's prophecy that he would carry people's sicknesses himself. After warning a would-be follower that following him meant having nowhere permanent to lay his head, Jesus calmed a violent storm on the Sea of Galilee with a word while his disciples panicked, and then, arriving in Gentile territory, cast demons out of two tormented men into a herd of pigs, which rushed into the sea and drowned, so unsettling the local people that they begged him to leave (Matthew 8:1-34).

## 📖 Core Story: Forgiving Sins, Calling Matthew, Raising the Dead

Jesus healed a paralyzed man by first forgiving his sins, demonstrating his authority to do both, which amazed the crowds. He then called the tax collector Matthew to follow him, and ate with him and other "sinners," defending the practice to critical Pharisees as a doctor's necessary work among the sick, and explaining to John's disciples that his presence was cause for celebration, not fasting, like a wedding rather than a funeral. When a synagogue ruler begged him to heal his dying daughter, Jesus went with him, healing a woman with a chronic bleeding disorder along the way through her faith alone, then raised the ruler's daughter from apparent death, taking her by the hand after dismissing mourners who laughed at him. He also healed two blind men who called him "Son of David" and freed a demon-possessed mute man, provoking both wonder from the crowds and hostile accusations from the Pharisees that he worked by the power of Satan. Moved with compassion for the crowds like a shepherdless flock, Jesus told his disciples the harvest was plentiful but workers were few (Matthew 9:1-38).

## 📖 Core Story: Naming and Sending the Twelve Apostles

Jesus named his twelve apostles — Peter, Andrew, James and John sons of Zebedee, Philip, Bartholomew, Thomas, Matthew, James son of Alphaeus, Thaddaeus, Simon the Zealot, and Judas Iscariot, who would later betray him — and gave them authority to heal and cast out demons, sending them first to Israel rather than Gentiles or Samaritans. He warned them of coming persecution, urged them not to fear those who could only kill the body, promised that confessing him before others would be rewarded, and acknowledged that following him would bring division even within families, since whoever loved family more than him, or clung to life rather than risking it for his sake, was not worthy of him (Matthew 10:1-42).

 When John, in prison, sent disciples to ask whether he was the Messiah, Jesus pointed to his healings as proof, then praised John to the crowds as the greatest person born of woman and the promised Elijah, while lamenting that this generation had rejected both John's asceticism and his own open table fellowship. He denounced the unrepentant cities where he had done miracles, declaring Capernaum, Chorazin, and Bethsaida more culpable than Sodom and Tyre, then thanked the Father for hiding deep truths from the proud while revealing them to the humble, and invited the weary to find rest by taking up his easy yoke (Matthew 11:1-30).

## 📖 Core Story: Lord of the Sabbath, Conflict with the Pharisees

When Pharisees criticized his disciples for picking grain on the Sabbath, Jesus cited David's precedent of eating consecrated bread and declared himself greater than the temple and Lord of the Sabbath; he then healed a man's withered hand on the Sabbath despite their hostility, provoking them to plot his death. After healing a demon-possessed, blind, and mute man, the Pharisees accused him of casting out demons by Satan's power; Jesus refuted the logic as self-defeating and warned that blasphemy against the Holy Spirit, unlike other sins, would not be forgiven. When asked for a miraculous sign, he refused, saying the only sign would be his own three days in the earth, as Jonah spent three days in the fish, and that the repentant Ninevites and the Queen of the South (who sought out Solomon's wisdom) would condemn his unrepentant generation on judgment day. When told his mother and brothers wanted to speak with him, Jesus declared that whoever did his Father's will was his true family (Matthew 12:1-50).

## 📖 Core Story: Parables of the Kingdom

Jesus taught the crowds in parables, explaining to his disciples that he did so to reveal truth to those receptive to it while concealing it from those who were not, fulfilling Isaiah's prophecy of a people who would hear but not understand. He told of a sower whose seed met different receptions depending on the soil, of wheat and weeds growing together until the harvest, and of the kingdom of heaven growing like a mustard seed or spreading like yeast, starting small but becoming great; he also compared the kingdom to a treasure or pearl worth selling everything to obtain, and to a net gathering both good and bad fish for a final sorting. When he returned to his hometown, the people, familiar with him as a carpenter's son whose mother was Mary and whose brothers were James, Joses, Simon, and Judas, took offense and refused to honor him as a prophet, limiting the miracles he did there (Matthew 13:1-58).

## 📖 Core Story: Feeding the Five Thousand and Walking on Water

Hearing of John's death, Jesus withdrew, but crowds followed; moved with compassion, he healed their sick and, with only five loaves and two fish, fed about five thousand men besides women and children, with twelve baskets of food left over. He then sent the disciples ahead by boat and went up a mountain alone to pray; during a night storm, he came to them walking on the water, and when Peter asked to join him, Peter walked briefly on the water too before fear made him begin to sink, until Jesus caught his hand, gently rebuking his doubt. When they reached the boat the wind ceased, and the disciples worshipped him as the Son of God (Matthew 14:13-36).

## 📖 Core Story: True Defilement and the Canaanite Woman's Faith

When Pharisees criticized his disciples for not washing their hands before eating, Jesus countered that their own traditions let them dishonor their parents, and taught that true defilement comes not from food but from the evil that proceeds from the heart — murder, adultery, theft, false witness, and the like. Traveling into Gentile territory near Tyre and Sidon, he was approached by a Canaanite woman begging him to heal her demon-possessed daughter; when he initially demurred, saying he was sent only to Israel, she persisted with a clever, humble reply, and Jesus, impressed by her great faith, healed her daughter. He then healed a great crowd and, moved with compassion for a multitude that had stayed with him three days without food, multiplied seven loaves and a few fish to feed about four thousand men besides women and children, with seven baskets left over (Matthew 15:1-39).

## 📖 Core Story: Peter's Confession and the First Prediction of the Cross

When Pharisees and Sadducees demanded a sign, Jesus again pointed only to the sign of Jonah, then warned his disciples against the corrupting "leaven" of the Pharisees' and Sadducees' teaching. At Caesarea Philippi, Jesus asked who people thought he was; after the disciples relayed various guesses, Peter declared him "the Christ, the Son of the living God." Jesus blessed Peter for this Father-given insight, declared he would build his church on this rock, and gave him the keys of the kingdom with authority to bind and loose. Jesus then began explaining that he must go to Jerusalem to suffer, die, and rise again; when Peter rebuked him for saying so, Jesus sharply called Peter "Satan" for thinking in merely human terms, and taught that true discipleship meant denying oneself and taking up one's cross, since gaining the world while losing one's soul profited nothing (Matthew 16:1-28).

## 📖 Core Story: The Transfiguration

Jesus took Peter, James, and John up a mountain, where he was transfigured before them, his face shining like the sun; Moses and Elijah appeared, speaking with him, and a voice from a bright cloud again declared him God's beloved Son, terrifying the disciples until Jesus reassured them. Coming down, Jesus explained that John the Baptist had fulfilled the role of the Elijah who was to come. He then healed a boy with a severe seizure disorder that his disciples had failed to cure, attributing their failure to lack of faith, and again predicted his coming betrayal, death, and resurrection, grieving his disciples. When tax collectors in Capernaum questioned Peter about the temple tax, Jesus had Peter catch a fish containing a coin exactly sufficient to pay the tax for them both, to avoid giving needless offense (Matthew 17:1-27).

## 📖 Core Story: Humility, Church Discipline, and Boundless Forgiveness

Jesus taught that greatness in the kingdom required becoming humble like a child, warned severely against causing others to stumble, and told the parable of a shepherd leaving ninety-nine sheep to search for one lost one to illustrate God's concern for the straying. He laid out a process for confronting a sinning believer privately, then with witnesses, and finally before the whole church, with authority given to bind and loose matters on earth and in heaven, promising his own presence wherever believers gathered in his name. When Peter asked how often he should forgive a repeatedly sinning brother, suggesting seven times, Jesus answered "seventy times seven," then told the parable of a servant forgiven an enormous debt who refused to forgive a much smaller debt owed to him, warning that God would likewise withhold mercy from those who withheld it from others (Matthew 18:1-35).

## 📖 Core Story: Marriage, Children, and the Rich Young Man

When Pharisees tested Jesus about divorce, he affirmed marriage as God's unbreakable design from creation, explaining that Moses had only permitted divorce because of human hardness of heart, and declared that divorcing a spouse except for sexual immorality and remarrying amounted to adultery. After welcoming children his disciples tried to turn away, declaring the kingdom belonged to such as these, Jesus was approached by a wealthy young man asking what he must do to gain eternal life; when the man claimed to have kept all the commandments, Jesus told him to sell his possessions and give to the poor, and the man left sorrowful, unwilling to part with his wealth. Jesus then taught how hard it is for the rich to enter the kingdom — like a camel through a needle's eye — though nothing is impossible for God. When Peter asked what reward the disciples who had given up everything to follow Jesus would receive, Jesus promised them thrones in the age to come and declared that the last would be first, and the first last (Matthew 19:1-30).

## 📖 Core Story: Workers in the Vineyard, Serving Rather Than Ruling

Jesus told the parable of a vineyard owner who hired workers at different hours of the day but paid them all the same generous wage, illustrating that God's grace is not earned by seniority or merit. On the way to Jerusalem, Jesus predicted his death and resurrection a third time; when James and John's mother asked that her sons sit at his right and left in his kingdom, Jesus told the brothers they would share his suffering but that such honors were the Father's to grant, and taught all twelve, after the other ten grew indignant, that true greatness meant serving others, since he himself had come not to be served but to serve and give his life as a ransom for many. Leaving Jericho, two blind men cried out to him as "Son of David" despite the crowd's rebukes, and Jesus, moved with compassion, restored their sight (Matthew 20:1-34).

## 📖 Core Story: The Triumphal Entry and Cleansing the Temple

Jesus rode into Jerusalem on a donkey as crowds hailed him with palm branches and shouts of "Hosanna to the Son of David," fulfilling Zechariah's prophecy of a humble king's arrival. He then drove out the merchants and money-changers from the temple, condemning them for turning a house of prayer into a den of thieves, and healed the blind and lame there despite the hostility of the chief priests and scribes, who were further provoked by children's praise of him. The next day, he cursed a fruitless fig tree, which withered instantly, teaching his disciples about the power of faith-filled prayer. When religious leaders demanded to know his authority, he countered by asking about John the Baptist's authority, which they couldn't answer without political risk, and so he declined to answer them directly. He then told the parable of two sons, one who refused his father's command but obeyed anyway and one who agreed but didn't, to show that repentant sinners would enter the kingdom before the self-righteous religious leaders, and the parable of the wicked tenants who killed the vineyard owner's son, warning that the kingdom would be taken from unfaithful leaders and given to others — parables the chief priests and Pharisees recognized as aimed at them, though fear of the crowds kept them from arresting him (Matthew 21:1-46).

## 📖 Core Story: Final Confrontations in the Temple

Jesus told the parable of a king's wedding feast whose invited guests refused to come and were destroyed, while outsiders were gathered in, only for one improperly dressed guest to be cast out, illustrating that many are called but few chosen. When Pharisees and Herodians tried to trap him over paying taxes to Caesar, he answered that people should give Caesar what bears Caesar's image and give God what bears God's. Sadducees, who denied the resurrection, posed a trick question about a widow married to seven brothers in turn; Jesus corrected their misunderstanding of resurrected life and affirmed the resurrection itself by noting that God called himself the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob — the living, not the dead. When a lawyer asked which was the greatest commandment, Jesus named loving God fully and loving one's neighbor as oneself, on which all the Law and Prophets depend; he then silenced his questioners by asking how David could call his own descendant, the Christ, "Lord" in the Psalms (Matthew 22:1-46).

Jesus then pronounced seven scathing "woes" against the scribes and Pharisees for their hypocrisy — performing righteousness for show, burdening others without helping, obsessing over minor legal details while neglecting justice and mercy, and outwardly appearing righteous while being inwardly corrupt, like a clean cup hiding filth or a beautifully adorned tomb full of bones. He charged them with the guilt of all the righteous blood shed throughout Israel's history, and ended with a lament over Jerusalem's unwillingness to be gathered to him like a mother hen gathers her chicks, warning that the city would be left desolate (Matthew 23:1-39).

## 📖 Core Story: The Olivet Discourse

Leaving the temple, Jesus predicted its total destruction; on the Mount of Olives, his disciples asked when this would happen and what would signal the end of the age. He warned of wars, famines, false prophets, and persecution as preliminary signs, and pointed to "the abomination of desolation" spoken of by Daniel as a marker of coming tribulation severe enough that it would be cut short for the elect's sake. He compared his return to lightning flashing across the sky — sudden and visible to all — and to the days of Noah, when people carried on ordinary life unaware of the coming flood until it was too late, urging constant readiness since no one knows the exact timing. He followed this with the parable of ten bridesmaids, five prepared and five not, to stress readiness; the parable of a man entrusting his servants with money ("talents") while away, rewarding those who invested wisely and condemning the one who did nothing out of fear; and finally the vision of a final judgment separating "sheep" from "goats" based on how they had treated the hungry, thirsty, strangers, needy, sick, and imprisoned — declaring that caring for "the least of these" was the same as caring for him personally (Matthew 24:1-25:46).

## 📖 Core Story: The Last Supper, Gethsemane, and Arrest

At the Passover meal, Jesus announced that one of the Twelve would betray him, and when Judas asked if it were he, Jesus confirmed it quietly. He instituted what became the Lord's Supper, identifying bread as his body and wine as his blood of the new covenant, poured out for the forgiveness of sins. After singing a hymn, they went to the Mount of Olives, where Jesus predicted all the disciples would desert him and that Peter specifically would deny him three times before dawn, despite Peter's confident denial. At Gethsemane, taking Peter, James, and John further with him, Jesus was overwhelmed with anguish and prayed three times that he might be spared the coming suffering while surrendering to the Father's will, finding his disciples asleep each time he returned. Judas then arrived with an armed crowd and betrayed Jesus with a kiss; when a disciple cut off the ear of the high priest's servant, Jesus rebuked the violence, healed the wound (per Luke), and submitted to arrest, noting that this fulfilled Scripture even as all his disciples fled. Brought before Caiaphas and the council, Jesus was accused by false witnesses and remained silent until directly asked whether he was the Christ; his admission that he was, and his claim to future glory, led Caiaphas to charge him with blasphemy, and the council condemned him to death, mocking and beating him (Matthew 26:17-68). Meanwhile Peter, who had followed at a distance, denied knowing Jesus three times exactly as predicted, and wept bitterly upon hearing the rooster crow (Matthew 26:69-75).

## 📖 Core Story: Trial Before Pilate, Crucifixion, and Burial

Handed over to the Roman governor Pilate, Jesus gave no answer to the chief priests' accusations, amazing Pilate. Warned by his wife's troubled dream and recognizing the charges came from envy, Pilate offered the crowd a choice between releasing Jesus or the notorious prisoner Barabbas; persuaded by the chief priests, the crowd demanded Barabbas's release and cried "Let him be crucified," accepting responsibility for his blood even as Pilate symbolically washed his hands of it. Jesus was scourged, mocked with a purple robe, a crown of thorns, and a reed scepter, and spat upon by Roman soldiers, who then led him away to be crucified, compelling Simon of Cyrene to carry his cross (Matthew 27:1-32).

At Golgotha, Jesus refused wine mixed with gall, was crucified between two criminals under a sign reading "THE KING OF THE JEWS," and was mocked by passersby, the chief priests, and the criminals alike for his claim to be God's Son. From the sixth to the ninth hour darkness covered the land, and Jesus cried out in the words of Psalm 22, "Eli, Eli, lama sabachthani" ("My God, my God, why have you forsaken me"), before crying out again and giving up his spirit. At the moment of his death the temple veil tore from top to bottom, the earth shook, tombs opened, and many dead saints were raised; a Roman centurion and the soldiers with him, witnessing these things, declared him truly the Son of God. Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James and Joses, and the mother of Zebedee's sons watched from a distance, having followed and ministered to Jesus from Galilee. Joseph of Arimathea, a wealthy disciple, asked Pilate for the body, wrapped it in clean linen, and laid it in his own new tomb cut into rock, rolling a stone across the entrance while the two Marys kept watch. The next day, the chief priests and Pharisees, remembering Jesus's predictions of rising after three days, asked Pilate to secure the tomb; Pilate had it sealed and set a guard (Matthew 27:33-66).
